# The Noise Between Stars

There's a specific kind of loneliness that doesn't announce itself. It sits quietly in the back of your throat on ordinary Tuesday afternoons, the kind where the light does something strange through your kitchen window and you realize there's no one to say, "Look at that," to.

I think about how the spaces between stars aren't actually empty. They're full — radiation, dust, the remnants of ancient explosions, gravitational whispers. The void is a misnomer. The void is the most populated room in the building.

We live our lives the same way. The silences between conversations, the pauses between breaths, the seconds that stretch between a text message sent and a reply received — these aren't nothing. They're everything. They're where the anxiety lives and where the imagination also lives. They're where you either remember you're human or forget you ever were.

I met a man once at a bus stop who told me he'd spent eleven years working on a single wood carving. A bird. He said it was almost done. He said he'd lost his left hand in an accident three months ago but was determined to finish with what remained. I asked him why he didn't start over, and he looked at me like I'd suggested he chew off his own foot. "Why would I start over?" he said. "This is the only one that knows where I've been."

I think about that carving sometimes. About what it looks like. About whether the one-handed version has a rawness that the original never would have had — some kind of honest asymmetry that the accident forced into existence.

We are all one-handed wood carvers, if we're honest. We all begin projects — relationships, careers, identities — with two hands and full expectations, and life takes something and we keep working anyway, and what emerges is neither what we planned nor a failure of the plan but something else entirely. Something that carries the whole story in its grain.

There's this phenomenon called the **overview effect** — the shift in perspective astronauts report when they see Earth from space. They describe a sudden, overwhelming sense of how small and fragile everything is, and simultaneously how precious. Borders vanish. Arguments become absurd. The petty machinery of daily life stops grinding.

But here's what strikes me: most of them also describe an aching, almost unbearable beauty. Not the clinical beauty of science or the manufactured beauty of a gallery painting, but the beauty of something you didn't choose and can't control. The beauty of existing inside a moment you could not possibly have engineered or predicted or manufactured through willpower alone.

We chase experiences the way he chased that carving — with intensity, with two-handed grip, with the belief that effort equals outcome. And often it does. But the overview effect doesn't come from effort. It comes from altitude. It comes from stepping outside the thing you were doing and seeing that the thing was always already inside something larger.

I think about this when I can't sleep. Which is often. I lie there and let the night do what night does — which is press every feeling against every other feeling until something gives. The grief edges into the gratitude. The fear folds into the wonder. And in that pressurized space, for just a moment, they become the same thing.

Maybe that's what the loneliness and the connection and the silence and the noise have in common. They're not opposites. They're the same room, seen from different angles. You just have to turn around.

The man at the bus stop never told me his name. The bus came. He nodded — once, deliberate, like someone confirming a fact — and climbed on. I watched it pull away, and I stood there longer than I needed to, and the evening did what evening does: it made everything look either more important or less, depending on where you were standing.

I was standing in the noise between stars. The void that was full. The silence that was saying something I couldn't quite hear but recognized anyway — the low, persistent hum of everything being alive at once, all of it, the whole absurd, beautiful, one-handed, unfinished bird of it, and the unbroken ache of not knowing if it's ever going to look the way we thought it would.

It won't. It never does. And thank god.
